analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 2010 Wall Street reform law in its entirety.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal Dodd-Frank, backed by 15 House Republicans, was referred to eight committees and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Dodd-Frank Act, the 2010 law passed after the financial crisis that tightened rules on banks and Wall Street firms, created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and gave the government tools to wind down failing financial firms. Repealing it would restore the regulatory framework that existed before the crisis. The bill was introduced at the start of the 112th Congress but never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, large banks, investment firms, derivatives traders, and other financial institutions would gain the most: they would be freed from Dodd-Frank's capital requirements, derivatives regulation, consumer protection rules, and the risk of being wound down through the Act's liquidation process instead of bankruptcy. Consumers would lose the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's oversight of mortgages, credit cards, and other financial products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large banks and Wall Street firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act in its entirety and revives or restores the provisions of law that the Act amended, as if Dodd-Frank had never been enacted.
Dodd-Frank's rules covered banking, securities, derivatives and commodities markets, and consumer financial protection, so repeal would remove all of those constraints on financial firms at once.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers would bear the risk. They would lose the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's ability to police mortgages, credit cards, and lending abuses, and the pre-2008 framework that the crisis exposed would return, leaving taxpayers once again exposed when large financial firms fail.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, removing the primary federal watchdog for mortgages, credit cards, and consumer lending, leaving consumers with far less recourse against abusive financial products.

It would restore the regulatory landscape as it existed before the 2008 crisis, the period whose failures Dodd-Frank was written to fix, by reviving the provisions of law as if the Act had not been enacted.

Repealing the entire Act would also unwind prudential rules for large banks and the orderly-liquidation framework, so failing financial giants would again face only bankruptcy or taxpayer-backed rescue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Financial institutions would gain by shedding a broad set of rules; consumers and taxpayers would lose a consumer watchdog and post-crisis safeguards. The bill was written as a clean, total repeal with no replacement framework, so the cost side is unmitigated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced, got no hearings or floor action, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Michele Bachmann and 14 Republican cosponsors introduced H.R. 87 on January 5, 2011, the first day of the 112th Congress, to repeal the Dodd-Frank Act in full.

The bill was referred to the Financial Services Committee plus seven other committees (Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Budget, Oversight and Government Reform, Ways and Means, and Small Business), and then to several subcommittees; it never advanced to a markup or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial institutions: the rules Dodd-Frank imposed remained on the books, but repeal proponents were no closer to removing them, and no investor-facing changes were made either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks kept the status quo; no rules changed

for.name: Michele Bachmann
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Dodd-Frank in full on the first day of the 112th Congress.

for.name: 14 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the repeal bill.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats backed the bill, and it never reached a vote in the Republican-held House or the Democratic-held Senate.

industries.industry: Banks and Wall Street financial firms
industries.note: Repeal would free banks and investment firms from Dodd-Frank's capital rules, derivatives regulation, and consumer protections, shifting risk back to consumers and taxpayers. The bill never advanced, so the industry's position under Dodd-Frank did not change.
Repeal would remove Dodd-Frank's new oversight of swaps and commodities markets, restoring the largely unregulated pre-2010 environment.

Repeal would abolish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and other consumer safeguards covering mortgages, credit cards, and lending, leaving households with weaker protection against abusive products.
